meta.title: Rookwood's Cincinnati clay
meta.summary: A tile can belong to a building and still be a little work of art. Cincinnati’s Rookwood makers have explored that since 1880. ♡

blocks.text: I’m taking you back to Cincinnati in 1880, when Maria Longworth Storer founded Rookwood with one kiln and a plan to make American art pottery. The first potters worked in a former schoolhouse, shaping clay from the Ohio River. Rookwood still makes pottery, tile, and custom work in Cincinnati. I love how the same care for form and surface can live in a vase on a table or a tile in a wall.

Rookwood describes a process in which many hands touch each piece before it is finished. That matters more to this story than treating every object as a museum relic. Glazes, shapes, and uses have changed, while people continue to make things for homes and public interiors. Look at a tile closely next time; its texture may tell you as much as its pattern. I’m drawn to a glaze that gathers differently along an edge. Show me the piece you’d linger over? I might need another look too. ♡
